author: Elisabeth Edwards
title: U.S. soldiers warned officials that Combat Outpost Keating in Afghanistan was in a dangerous location, which made it vulnerable to a Taliban attack - NewsBreak
text: On October 3, 2009, Combat Outpost Keating in Kamdesh, Afghanistan, became the site of one of the most intense battles of the war. Perched in a remote valley near the Pakistan border, the outpost was suddenly attacked by more than 300 well-armed Taliban fighters. Defending it were just 50 U.S. soldiers from Black Knight Troop, 3rd Squadron, 61st Cavalry Regiment, part of the 4th Infantry Division. What followed was a harrowing fight for survival. The insurgents launched a coordinated assault from all sides, unleashing relentless gunfire and RPGs. With the enemy closing in, the battle devolved into brutal close-quarters combat. Despite being outnumbered more than six to one, the American troops held their ground through sheer grit and determination. The cost was steep—eight U.S. soldiers were killed and 22 wounded. Yet, the defenders’ bravery turned what could have been a total defeat into a display of unwavering resolve. Their actions earned numerous commendations, including two Medals of Honor, and COP Keating became a lasting symbol of courage under fire. Combat Outpost Keating was established in 2006 in Afghanistan’s remote Nuristan province, nestled deep in the isolated Landai Sin Valley. From the outset, its position raised red flags among U.S. soldiers. Surrounded by steep, forested mountains, the base sat at the bottom of a natural bowl—leaving it exposed to enemy fire from above. Resupply efforts were equally hazardous, with narrow, poorly maintained roads and unpredictable terrain forcing reliance on dangerous nighttime helicopter missions. Despite its vulnerabilities, the outpost held undeniable strategic value. Located near the Pakistan border at the junction of three critical valleys, COP Keating was ideally placed to monitor and disrupt insurgent supply routes. Its role was to choke off the flow of weapons and fighters into Afghanistan and to challenge Taliban influence in the region. At the heart of its mission was a counterinsurgency strategy focused on outreach and development. U.S. forces worked to earn local support through aid initiatives, infrastructure projects, and direct engagement. Still, Taliban forces remained active and entrenched nearby, frequently targeting the base with everything from small arms fire to coordinated assaults. By mid-2009, military leadership determined that the costs of maintaining COP Keating outweighed its strategic advantages. Plans were made to shut it down by the fall. However, a combination of logistical delays, worsening road conditions, and political complications between Washington and Kabul stalled the withdrawal. The Taliban took full advantage of this window. In the first nine months of 2009 alone, the outpost was hit with more than 200 attacks. As conditions deteriorated and reinforcements remained out of reach, the troops of Black Knight Troop found themselves increasingly isolated—setting the stage for the catastrophic assault on October 3, 2009. In the early hours of October 3, 2009, around 3:00 AM, roughly 300 Taliban-backed insurgents arrived near Kamdesh, ordering local villagers to evacuate the area. After concluding their morning prayers, the attackers unleashed a fierce assault on Combat Outpost Keating using Soviet-era B-10 recoilless rifles, DShK heavy machine guns, rocket-propelled grenades (RPGs), and mortar fire. The insurgents demonstrated intimate knowledge of the outpost’s layout and weaponry, immediately focusing their assault on the base’s most formidable defense—the 120 mm mortar. As the attackers advanced on COP Keating, other forces targeted nearby Observation Post Fritsche. At 6:03 AM, Fritsche sent a distress signal: “FRITSCHE AND KEATING IN HEAVY CONTACT.” Within minutes, the first American casualty occurred—Private First Class Kevin Thomson was fatally shot in the face while defending the northernmost mortar pit. Soon after, Sergeant Josh Kirk suffered injuries from RPG shrapnel while preparing to fire an AT4 anti-tank rocket, and moments later, a sniper’s bullet struck him in the head. Despite attempts to fight back from armored Humvees equipped with mounted machine guns, U.S. troops were overwhelmed as their ammunition began to dwindle. Sergeant Vernon Martin was wounded by gunfire, and shortly after, an RPG blast dislodged a .50 caliber machine gun from its mount, causing shrapnel wounds to Martin as well. Martin and another soldier were near a Humvee when Sergeant Justin Gallegos and Specialist Stephen Mace joined them inside. Specialist Ty Carter heroically dashed through heavy enemy fire, carrying ammunition to repair the Humvee’s disabled M240 machine gun . With the primary defense compromised, COP Keating became increasingly vulnerable to the insurgent assault. Specialist Michael Scusa was killed by a bullet to the neck while rushing from the barracks to reinforce another position. Staff Sergeant Clinton Romesha, trying to provide cover for the trapped soldiers in the Humvee, opened fire with his M48 machine gun but sustained injuries amid the relentless enemy onslaught. Forty-eight minutes into the Battle of Kamdesh, the Taliban broke through the perimeter defenses of COP Keating. The Afghan National Army soldiers, who were assigned to guard positions around the base, were urged to stand their ground but ultimately fled as the fighting grew more intense. American troops reported that none of the Afghan soldiers stayed; instead, they ran away, hid, or took equipment and supplies from the base during and after the attack. The Taliban entered the compound and set important buildings on fire. About an hour into the battle, the defenders of COP Keating retreated to secure the last two buildings as the enemy took over more of the base. With the number of Taliban fighters increasing, the remaining U.S. soldiers realized they were at risk of being completely overrun. Lt. Andrew Bundermann ordered the troops to pull back, tighten the perimeter, and focus their firepower.
